During a stroke, a series of biochemical and metabolic changes occur which eventually lead to the death of cells by necrosis or apoptosis. This is a multi-stage process involving oxidative stress and an inflammatory response from the first signs of occlusion of a blood vessel until the late stages of regeneration and healing of ischemic tissues. The purpose of the research was to assess the concentration of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α in the blood serum of patients with ischemic stroke (AIS) and to investigate their role as new markers in predicting functional prognosis after thrombolytic therapy. The researches have shown that the concentrations of the measured biomarkers were higher compared to the control group. Serum levels of IL-6 and THF-α before the initiation of intravenous thrombolysis were lower in the subgroup of patients with a favourable functional result (mRS: 0–2 pts) compared to the group of patients with an unfavourable functional result (mRS: 3–6 pts). A positive correlation was found between the concentration of IL-6 and TNF-α in patients with AIS during <4.5 h and on one day after the onset of stroke, which means that the concentration of IL-6 increases with the increase in TNF-α concentration. It has also been shown that higher levels of IL-6 in the acute phase of stroke and on the first and seventh days, and TNF-α during onset, were associated with poorer early and late prognosis in patients treated with intravenous thrombolysis. A relationship was found between the level of IL-6 and TNF-α in the subacute AIS and the severity of the neurological deficit. It has been shown that the investigated biomarkers may be a prognostic factor in the treatment of thrombolytic AIS. ischemic stroke interleukin-6 tumor necrosis factor modified Rankin Scale National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale Nicolaus Copernicus University 10/2022 Research Project, Collegium Medicum This work has been supported by Nicolaus Copernicus University as part of the Initiative of excellence competition-Research University-“Debuts” (10/2022) and Research Project, Collegium Medicum in 2022. 1. Introduction Stroke is the second leading cause of death and permanent disability, after the heart attack, in people above forty. The origins of the stroke could be related to heart embolism, cerebral microangiopathy, haematological diseases, as well as extracranial and intracranial arteriosclerosis [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]. During a stroke, there is a risk of rupturing blood vessels and bleeding in some parts of the brain. Therefore, the strokes can be classified as ischemic or haemorrhagic, which comprise about 85% and 15% of the reported cases, respectively [ 3 ]. Patients who survive the acute phase of the disease require intensive care due to physical, verbal, and intellectual disability. The neurological scale is employed as a tool to measure the degree of damage caused by a stroke. During a stroke, a lack of blood flow in the ischemic core of the brain is responsible for a decrease in the oxygen, glucose, and lipids supplied to the brain neurons and other neighbouring cells and tissues. This causes several different biochemical and metabolic changes, which eventually lead to the death of cells by necrosis or apoptosis [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ]. This is a multi-layered, complex, and surging process which involves oxidative stress and inflammation from the first signs of occlusion of a blood vessel until the late stages of regeneration and healing of ischemic tissues [ 5 , 6 , 7 ]. Consequently, the microvessels are damaged as well as glial, and neuronal cells are activated. In addition, a dysfunction in the brain–blood barrier (BBB) and leukocyte infiltration is observed. Brain damage not only increases the inflammation in the ischemic brain but is also responsible for the systemic immunological reaction concurrent with lymphocytopenia that causes immunodepression [ 6 ]. However, the immunological response of the body remains a controversial issue and the subject of many arguments, especially whether the role of the immune system carries beneficial or harmful consequences [ 9 ]. There is an opinion that the immune system can act as a promising and important tool employed in the modulation of brain injury during and after a stroke. However, despite the extensive research, no significant indicators (markers) have been selected as the ones which could successfully prevent, detect, and treat strokes. It has been proven that excitotoxicity and an increase in the reactive oxygen species (ROS) cause an expression of many pro-inflammatory genes by the excitation of various transcription factors. In addition, the activated microglia and astrocytes give rise to the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, anti-inflammatory chemokines, and matrix metalloproteinases (MMP) [ 7 , 9 , 10 ]. At the surface of the endothelium, inflammatory mediators induce the expression of cell adhesion that mediates the adherence of leukocytes to the lesion site [ 6 ]. The influence of inflammatory bio-markers on the long-term prognosis of patients treated with rt-PA (recombinant tissue plasminogen activator) employed in intravenous thrombolytic and endovascular therapy remains an object of controversy. It has been suggested that molecules that affect a patient’s prognosis are cytokines such as interleukin-1 (IL-1), interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α). However, there is no clear information related to their concentrations and their overall effect on cerebral infarction. This research aims to illustrate the involvement of inflammation biomarkers such as IL-6 and TNF-α in the aetiology of acute ischemic stroke. The data was collected from the group of patients at different time intervals, namely < 4.5 h on the first and seventh day since the stroke, and compared with the results obtained from the group of healthy participants (control group) which allowed for the evaluation of those inflammation biomarkers as novel factors used in predicting functional prognosis after thrombolytic therapy. Careful analysis of these parameters will also help better comprehend how inflammation contributes to the progression of stroke in cerebral circulation disorders. This can be recognised as a valuable indication for modulating immune response mechanisms to limit damage to nervous tissue following ischemia.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigates the concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α in the blood serum/plasma of acute ischemic stroke (AIS) patients, particularly those undergoing intravenous thrombolytic therapy, compared to healthy controls. It aims to assess their prognostic value for functional outcomes, neurological disability, stroke severity, and mortality, as well as their involvement in the inflammatory response following stroke and variations across stroke subtypes. The findings highlight higher levels of these biomarkers in AIS patients, their correlation with poorer prognosis, and their potential as markers for stroke severity and therapeutic effectiveness. The document also suggests that infarct severity and volume relate to inflammatory response in cerebral hypoxia, and emphasizes the necessity for future, larger studies on anti-inflammatory strategies and the impact of these biomarkers on thrombolytic therapy prognosis.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily focused on observing biomarker levels in acute ischemic stroke patients, often in the context of intravenous thrombolysis. Specific details regarding the dose, intensity, or duration of thrombolytic therapy were not provided, nor were dose-response comparisons reported. Biomarker measurements were taken at multiple time points post-stroke/thrombolysis (e.g., <4.5h, 24h, 7 days, 3 months, 1 year) and correlated with functional outcomes and other clinical indicators.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher compared to the control group (e.g., 6.37 pg/mL [<4.5 h], 7.09 pg/mL [day 1], 6.54 pg/mL [day 7] vs. 3.59 pg/mL in control; all p<0.001); confirmed significant increase in serum levels within a few hours up to the 90th day after stroke; highest levels observed within the first 24 h. Lower in patients with a favorable functional result (mRS: 0–2 pts) compared to the group with an unfavorable functional result (mRS: 3–6 pts) before intravenous thrombolysis (e.g., <4.5h: 4.69 IQR 3.69–6.64 vs 6.48 IQR 5.81–8.70 pg/mL, p=0.012; 24h: 5.92 IQR 3.84–6.52 vs 10.0 IQR 7.38–11.6 pg/mL, p<0.001; 3 months: 5.82 IQR 3.79–6.51 vs 10.8 IQR 7.23–13.5 pg/mL, p<0.001; 1 year: 5.92 IQR 3.87–6.57 vs 12.4 IQR 11.1–14.6 pg/mL, p<0.001); statistically significant differences after 24 h for mRS: 0–2 pts and mRS: 3–6 pts both at admission, discharge and after three months, and after 7 days only at admission. Positive correlation with TNF-α concentration in patients with AIS during <4.5 h and on one day after stroke onset. Higher levels in the acute phase of stroke and on the first and seventh days, and high plasma levels in post-stroke patients, were associated with poorer initial and late prognosis in patients treated with intravenous thrombolysis and expansive ischemic lesions. Lower in LACI stroke subtype (e.g., 5.59 pg/mL) compared to PACI (7.29 pg/mL) at <4.5 h (p=0.016); lower serum concentrations in lacunar stroke compared to other AIS etiology. Initial levels correlate with the severity of stroke (size of the lesion), perfusion-weighted imaging (PWI) signal, and the patient’s neurological score. Inverse relationship between early IL-6 levels, the size of the lesion, and the neurological result (conflicting report by Sotgiu et al.). Higher concentration in cardio-embolic stroke patients (Licatai et al.). Concentration above 4 pg/mL determined on the 7th day after stroke, or a level of 6.470 pg/mL, indicates a high probability of death and reduced survival rate.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Mediates inflammation; pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion by activated microglia and astrocytes; modulates infarct evolution in experimental stroke; pro-inflammatory role in early inflammation in the central nervous system; inflammatory marker of acutely ischemic brain injury; involved in immuno-inflammatory activation; reflects distinct pathophysiology of stroke subtypes; inflammatory factor; some reports suggest a neuroprotective effect.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) patients, before and after initiation of intravenous thrombolysis; acute phase of stroke, one and seven days after stroke onset, subacute AIS; relating to functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale, mRS); AIS onset and early post-stroke phase; based on stroke subtype (LACI vs PACI vs POCI, lacunar stroke vs other AIS etiology); post-stroke complications leading to mortality; first day after a stroke; initial phase of stroke (Sotgiu et al. study); cardio-embolic stroke.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Prognostic factor for functional prognosis after thrombolytic therapy; associated with poorer early and late prognosis; related to the severity of neurological deficit in subacute AIS. Associated with better functional recovery post-stroke; indicates an inflammatory response in acute ischemic stroke; differentiates inflammatory response based on stroke subtype; predicts increased mortality risk in AIS patients. Associated with deterioration of functional status and a greater extent of the ischemic focus; correlates with stroke severity. Lower levels associated with a favourable functional outcome; higher levels associated with an unfavourable functional outcome (mRS 3-6 pts); lower levels observed in LACI-type AIS and lacunar stroke compared to other subtypes. Associated with an increased neurological deficit at admission and a higher degree of acute phase immuno-inflammatory activation; indicator of high probability of death and reduced survival rate. Concentrations at onset and on day 1 demonstrate good sensitivity and specificity in predicting functional outcomes after discharge (cut-off: 7.11 pg/mL), after 90 days (cut-off: 6.54 pg/mL), and after 1 year (cut-off: 8.55 pg/mL).

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher, lower, positive correlation, varied/conflicting, increased
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher compared to the control group (e.g., 42.4 pg/mL [<4.5 h], 46.2 pg/mL [day 1], 33.9 pg/mL [day 7] vs. 29.8 pg/mL in control). Lower in patients with a favorable functional result (mRS: 0–2 pts) compared to the group with an unfavorable functional result (mRS: 3–6 pts) before intravenous thrombolysis (e.g., <4.5h for discharge: 36.4 IQR 31.0–49.0 vs 50.2 IQR 45.0–52.5 pg/mL, p=0.010; 3 months: 33.9 IQR 31.0–46.5 vs 51.8 IQR 48.6–59.6 pg/mL, p<0.001; 1 year: 33.9 IQR 30.9–46.5 vs 52.5 IQR 49.1–56.0 pg/mL, p=0.006); also lower at 24h post-stroke in favorable outcome group after 1 year (43.3 IQR 34.1–50.0 vs 68.4 IQR 64.6–72.3 pg/mL, p=0.017); statistically important differences in concentration < 4.5 h in the subgroup of patients with a favourable functional result in comparison to patients with an unfavourable result at the time of discharge from the hospital, after three months and after a year; levels assessed after 24 h showed differences only after a year (implying higher for unfavourable outcome). Positive correlation with IL-6 concentration in patients with AIS during <4.5 h and on one day after stroke onset. Higher levels during onset were associated with poorer early and late prognosis. Conflicting reports of stroke-induced changes, with some showing increase within 24 and 48 h after stroke, followed by a slow decrease within 72 and 144 h, while others show unchanged levels. Elevated levels facilitated several biochemical processes. Lower in LACI patients (33.43 pg/mL) vs PACI patients (49.60 pg/mL) at <4.5h (p=0.017); also lower in LACI patients (33.43 pg/mL) vs POCI patients (48.82 pg/mL) at onset (p=0.04), and LACI (37.24 pg/mL) vs POCI (48.86 pg/mL) on day 1 (p=0.018); lower serum concentrations in lacunar stroke compared to other AIS etiology. Higher concentration in cardio-embolic stroke patients (Licatai et al.). Concentration > 37 pg/mL determined on the 7th day after stroke, or exceeding 50 pg/mL within 1 day after stroke, may indicate a high probability of death in patients. Increased plasma levels determined on admission correlated with the volume and severity of the stroke and the functional outcome of the patient. Correlation between levels measured during the onset time, with the NIHSS scale on admission, and mRS assessed in the third month after stroke. Relationship between the level and the risk of recurrent infarction was demonstrated by Welsh et al., occurring only in people with very high concentrations.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Prognostic factor for functional prognosis after thrombolytic therapy; associated with poorer early and late prognosis; related to the severity of neurological deficit in subacute AIS. Associated with better functional recovery and lower neurologic disability post-stroke; indicates an inflammatory response in acute ischemic stroke; differentiates inflammatory response based on stroke subtype; predicts increased mortality risk in AIS patients. Important for the effectiveness of therapy in AIS patients; indicates a pro-inflammatory role in the central nervous system; putative marker of stroke severity and neurological outcomes in humans. Correlates with clinical improvement (when decreasing); can be used as a useful prognostic indicator; contradictory results on correlation with stroke severity. Higher levels associated with an unfavourable functional outcome; correlates with stroke volume, severity, and functional outcome; potential marker of the extent of ischemic brain injury and its clinical consequences; lower levels observed in LACI-type AIS and lacunar stroke compared to other subtypes. Associated with an increased neurological deficit at admission and a higher degree of acute phase immuno-inflammatory activation; indicator of high probability of death. Associated with an increased risk of recurrent infarction in individuals with very high concentrations. Levels at <4.5h and on day 1 showed good sensitivity and specificity for evaluating neurologic disability at 3 months (<4.5h cut-off: 39.94 pg/mL; day 1 cut-off: 60.14 pg/mL) and 1 year (<4.5h cut-off: 42.54 pg/mL; day 1 cut-off: 60.14 pg/mL).
